|name=Aurebesh}}
{{Quote|These symbols are in our own language&mdash;Aurebesh&hellip;|[[Je'daii Temple Master]] [[Quan-Jang]]|<ref name="Dawn of the Jedi: Force Storm 3">[[Dawn of the Jedi: Force Storm 3|''Dawn of the Jedi: Force Storm'' 3]]</ref>}}
'''Aurebesh''' was a [[Writing/Legends|writing system]] commonly used to represent the [[Galactic Basic Standard/Legends|Basic]] [[Language/Legends|language]]. Its name was a portmanteau of its first two letters, [[Aurek/Legends|Aurek]] and [[Besh/Legends|Besh]]. Aurebesh was commonly used by major governments from the [[Galactic Empire/Legends|Galactic Empire]] to the [[Confederacy of Independent Systems/Legends|Confederacy of Independent Systems]].

==History==
===Pre-Republic origins===
{{Quote|These symbols are a designation&mdash;marked on our skin by our Rakatan masters.|The [[Force Hound]] [[Tau (individual)|Xesh]]|<ref name="Dawn of the Jedi: Force War 2">[[Dawn of the Jedi: Force War 2|''Dawn of the Jedi: Force War'' 2]]</ref>}}
[[File:RevanfindsStarMap.png|thumb|left|A Rakatan Star Map bearing pre&ndash;Aurebesh letters]]
Aurebesh was possibly more ancient than the [[Rakata/Legends|Rakatan]] [[Infinite Empire/Legends|Infinite Empire]]. While the Rakata used a logographic [[Rakatan writing system]], they named and marked the [[Force Hound]]s according to characters from that script. Meanwhile, a form of Aurebesh was known to the [[Tythan]]s, who, remaining isolated in the [[Settled Worlds]] of the [[Tython system/Legends|Tython system]] since [[36,453 BBY]], were not part of the Empire.<ref>[[Dawn of the Jedi: Force Storm 1|''Dawn of the Jedi: Force Storm'' 1]]</ref> Despite this, when contact was made between the Tythans and the Rakata ([[25,793 BBY]]) the Rakatan Aurebesh was apparently identical to that used in the Settled Worlds: the Force Hound [[Tau (individual)|known as]] "Xesh" crashed on [[Tython/Legends|Tython]], and when the [[Je'daii]] found him, they were surprised to recognise the character [[Xesh/Legends|Xesh]] [[Tattoo/Legends|tattooed]] on his body.<ref name="Dawn of the Jedi: Force Storm 3" /><ref name="Dawn of the Jedi: The Prisoner of Bogan 1">[[Dawn of the Jedi: The Prisoner of Bogan 1|''Dawn of the Jedi: The Prisoner of Bogan'' 1]]</ref>

In any case, the Rakatan writing system was introduced to [[The galaxy/Legends|the galaxy]] at large during that Empire's reign and it was thought to be responsible for the development of Aurebesh. Enslaved species imitated the shapes of glyphs to develop their own, generally without taking into account the original usage or values of the glyphs.<ref name="WW">{{Hyperspace|url=hyperspace/source/writtenword/index.html?page=1|text=The Written Word|int=The Written Word}}</ref>

===Spread from Coruscant===
More modern forms of Aurebesh traced their origin to [[Coruscant/Legends|Coruscant]], as used for the [[Coruscanti/Legends|Coruscanti]] [[Old Galactic Standard]]. In the first millennium of the [[Galactic Republic/Legends|Galactic Republic]], Aurebesh coexisted with other individual writings among [[starship/Legends|starships]]; politics resisted the replacement of native script by the standard Galactic [[capital/Legends|Capital]]. However, on the wake of the [[Tionese War]], [[star system/Legends|systems]] from [[Corellian system/Legends|Corellia]] to [[Foerost system/Legends|Foerost]], urgently unified and furiously prepared new ships for the [[Republic Navy/Legends|Republic Navy]]; for practical reasons they resolved to adopting the Aurebesh for military use as universally recognisable. After that, Aurebesh enjoyed ubiquitous use and continued spreading throughout the [[Galactic Republic/Legends|Republic]], partly thanks to [[Merchant/Legends|traders]] of the late [[Expansionist_Period/Legends|Expansionist Period]].<ref name="WW" />

In the economic and political theater of the [[Alsakan Conflicts/Legends|Alsakan Conflicts]], the [[Alsakanese]] challenged Coruscant's cultural primacy; they promoted the [[Alsakan/Legends|Alsakan]]'s [[High Galactic (language)|High Galactic language]] and indpendent [[High Galactic/Legends|script]] as a rival to [[Galactic Basic Standard/Legends|Basic]] and the Aurebesh.<ref name="WW" />

Coruscant was for long believed to be the origin of the script. Despite this, there were variant systems, such as different values of letters, or flipped/rotated glyphs. Similar systems were also found among uncontacted [[alien/Legends|alien]] [[species/Legends|species]]; this family of scripts was believed to be one of the remnants of the [[Pre-Republic era|Pre-Republic]] Infinite Empire. Archaeologists came to that conclusion while studying Rakatan artifacts bearing glyphs similar to Aurebesh.<ref name="WW" />

Aurebesh text could be seen on the screens of various types of technology, including screens in the cockpits of [[N-1 starfighter/Legends|N-1 starfighters]],<ref name="Episode I">{{Film|I}}</ref> the [[Confederacy of Independent Systems/Legends|Separatist]] facility known as [[Skytop Station/Legends|Skytop Station]],<ref name="SWArchive-''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide: Duel of the Droids">{{SWArchive|url=theclonewars/guide/episode007.html|text=''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide: Duel of the Droids}}</ref> and inside [[Macrobinoculars/Legends|macrobinoculars]].<ref name="Ambush">{{SWArchive|url=theclonewars/guide/episode001.html|text=''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide: Ambush}}</ref><ref name="EG1">''[[Star Wars: The Clone Wars – The Official Episode Guide: Season 1]]''</ref><ref name="EG1&2">''[[Star Wars: The Clone Wars Official Episode Guide Series 1 & 2]]''</ref> Similarly, the [[Grand Army of the Republic/Legends|Grand Army of the Republic's]] tactical readouts made heavy use of Aurebesh text.<ref name="DoaD">{{SWArchive|url=theclonewars/guide/episode006.html|text=''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide: Downfall of a Droid}}</ref><ref name="EG1" /><ref name="EG1&2" /> Aurebesh was also used in medical settings<ref name="JC">{{SWArchive|url=theclonewars/guide/episode013.html|text=''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide: Jedi Crash}}</ref> and on wanted posters found in the [[Jedi Archives/Legends|Jedi Archives]].<ref name="SWArchive-''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide: Lightsaber Lost">{{SWArchive|url=theclonewars/guide/episode211.html|text=''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide: Lightsaber Lost}}</ref>

===Graffiti and tattoos during the Clone Wars===
[[Clone trooper/Legends|Clone troopers]] used it to mark their [[Low Altitude Assault Transport/Legends|LAAT gunships]] such as [[Lucky Lekku/Legends|''Lucky Lekku'']] and [[Spaceward Ho!/Legends|''Spaceward Ho!'']], both of which had their names painted on their sides,<ref name="10 Things in TCW 7">{{SWArchive|url=kids/read/cwspotter20080822.html|text=Checklist: 10 Things to Spot in ''The Clone Wars''}}</ref><ref name="SWArchive-''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide: Storm Over Ryloth">{{SWArchive|url=theclonewars/guide/episode019.html|text=''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide: Storm Over Ryloth}}</ref> or the [[Crumb Bomber/Legends|''Crumb Bomber'']], on which "Laugh this off" was inscribed.<ref name="SWArchive-Checklist: 10 Things to Spot in ''The Clone Wars''">{{SWArchive|url=kids/read/cwspotter20080822.html|text=Checklist: 10 Things to Spot in ''The Clone Wars''}} – The guide says "Laugh this off!," with an exclamation point</ref> Private starships also sometimes bore their names in Aurebesh, including the [[Freighter/Legends|freighter]] [[Tecora/Legends|''Tecora'']].<ref name="Kidnapped">{{SW|url=explore/the-clone-wars/ep411|text="Kidnapped" - ''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide"|nolive=1}} {{C|slide 4}}</ref>

The clone trooper [[Sketch/Legends|Sketch]] had a letter [[Senth/Legends|senth]] tattooed across his brow.<ref name="Star Wars: The Clone Wars Character Encyclopedia">''[[Star Wars: The Clone Wars Character Encyclopedia]]''</ref> [[Kix/Legends|Kix]]<ref name="TD">{{SWArchive|url=theclonewars/guide/episode210.html|text=''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide: The Deserter}}</ref><ref name="EG1&2" /> and the owner of [[Plop Dribble's/Legends|Plop Dribble's]] also had Aurebesh tattoos.<ref name="SW-Brothers - ''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide">{{SW|url=explore/the-clone-wars/ep421|text="Brothers" - ''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide|nolive=1}} {{C|Slide 7}}</ref> Similarly, the trooper [[Ponds/Legends|Ponds]] wrote "some guys have all the luck" on his armor.<ref name="LoR">{{SWArchive|url=theclonewars/guide/episode021.html|text=''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide: Liberty on Ryloth}}</ref> After his death, [[Fives/Legends|Fives]] and [[Echo/Legends|Echo]] both added decals to their armor that read "[[Hevy/Legends|Hevy]]."<ref name="SWArchive-''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide: ARC Troopers">{{SWArchive|url=theclonewars/guide/episode302.html|text=''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide: ARC Troopers}}</ref>

The [[Electro-proton bomb/Legends|electro-proton bomb]], attached to [[Goji/Legends|Goji]] and [[Rod/Legends|Rod's]] [[BTL-B Y-wing starfighter/Legends|bomber]] and dropped during the [[Battle of Malastare/Legends|Battle of Malastare]], had a warning printed on the nose cone that read "CAUTION ION DETONATOR." The body of the bomb had "CODE SWITCH DESIGNATOR" • "POSITION 1" • "POSITION 2" • "POSITION 3" • "POSITION 4" printed on it and on one of the tail fins, the words "THIS IS FOR YOU [[Dooku/Legends|DOOKU]]" were handwritten.<ref name="SWArchive-''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide: The Zillo Beast">{{SWArchive|url=theclonewars/guide/episode218.html|text=''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide: The Zillo Beast}}</ref>

Buildings were often marked with Aurebesh signs. These included [[Kristall Skull/Legends|Kristall Skull]] on [[Iego/Legends|Iego]]<ref name="MoaTM">{{SWArchive|url=theclonewars/guide/episode018.html|text=''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide: Mystery of a Thousand Moons}}</ref> and [[Chalmun's Spaceport Cantina/Legends|Chalmun's Spaceport Cantina]] on [[Tatooine/Legends|Tatooine]].<ref name="SWArchive-''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide: Corruption">{{SWArchive|url=theclonewars/guide/episode305.html|text=''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide: Corruption}}</ref> Many other companies used Aurebesh text on posters<ref name="Deception">{{SW|url=series/clone-wars/deception-trivia-gallery|text="Deception" Trivia Gallery}} {{C|Slide 5}}</ref> or billboards, such as one that promoted [[Star Tours/Legends|Star Tours]], which read "STAR TOURS [[Glee Anselm|GLEE ANSELM]] CALL 1-800-555-6576 NOW!"<ref name="Billboard">{{SWArchive|url=theclonewars/news20100121ads/index.html|text=Coruscant Billboard from ''The Clone Wars''}}</ref>

At [[Hondo's complex/Legends|Hondo Ohnaka's camp]] on [[Florrum/Legends|Florrum]], a huge piece of superstructure had "HONDO'S SALVAGE" – "PRICES SLASHED" stenciled on it in Aurebesh.<ref name="SW-Revival - ''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide">{{SW|url=explore/the-clone-wars/ep501|text="Revival" - ''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide|nolive=1}} {{C|Slide 6}}</ref> Meanwhile, around the time of the [[Bombing of the Jedi Temple hangar/Legends|Bombing of the Jedi Temple Hangar]], protesters carried Aurebesh signs that read "THE JEDI ARE CORRUPT" and "STOP CLONING VIOLENCE!"<ref name="SW-Sabotage - ''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide">{{SW|url=explore/the-clone-wars/ep517|text="Sabotage" - ''The Clone Wars'' Episode Guide|nolive=1}} {{C|Slide 8}}</ref>
===Imperial Era===
{{Quote|Aurebesh is for the common folk. Snobs like Villachor are way too upper-level for that.|[[Lando Calrissian/Legends|Lando Calrissian]], to [[Tavia Kitik]]|<ref name="Scoundrels" />}}
[[Luke Skywalker/Legends|Luke Skywalker]] learned to read Aurebesh by the time he was four years old, from a set of old educational [[Data-tape/Legends|datatapes]] given to him by his aunt [[Beru Whitesun Lars/Legends|Beru]].<ref name="A New Hope: The Life of Luke Skywalker">''[[A New Hope: The Life of Luke Skywalker]]''</ref>

Generally, Aurebesh was considered to be for the common folk, whereas the [[High Galactic/Legends|High Galactic alphabet]] was associated with snobbery.<ref name="Scoundrels">''[[Scoundrels]]''</ref>

==Features==
Aurebesh implemented consonants, vowels, digraphs, and punctuation marks. Words were separated by spaces. Aurebesh could be written mainly left-to-right or up-to-down. All letters are the same relative size, although occasionally symbols were mirror-inverted to denote capital letters. The symbol for the [[Galactic Republic/Legends|Republic]] [[Galactic Credit Standard/Legends|Credit]] was a [[Resh/Legends|Resh]] ('''R''' for '''R'''epublic) with two vertical lines through the upper half of the symbol. Letters of the alphabet were also used to denote musical keys, such as the [[key of Cresh]].

While the Aurebesh had several glyphs that corresponded to digraphs in the High Galactic alphabet, they were frequently disregarded. For example, the sound "oo,"<ref name="Star Wars Gamemaster Screen, Revised">''[[Star Wars Gamemaster Screen, Revised]]''</ref> which was properly noted using [[Orenth/Legends|Orenth]], was frequently spelled with a double [[Osk/Legends|Osk]].<ref name="S&V">[[Scum and Villainy (sourcebook)|''Scum and Villainy'']]</ref> Similarly, the letter [[Thesh/Legends|Thesh]] was often replaced by a combination of [[Trill/Legends|Trill]] and [[Herf/Legends|Herf]].<ref name="SW14">[[Star Wars (2013) 14|''Star Wars'' (2013) 14]]</ref> Such was also the case for [[Cherek/Legends|Cherek]] and [[Shen (letter)|Shen]], often written respectively with combinations of [[Cresh/Legends|Cresh]] and Herf and [[Senth/Legends|Senth]] and Herf.<ref name="EP">{{TCW|Evil Plans}}</ref>

==Behind the scenes==
===Evolution===
[[File:Aurebesh_2004.png|thumb|right|250px|The tractor beam information gauge, as it appears in the original [[Star Wars: Episode IV A New Hope|''Star Wars'': Episode IV ''A New Hope'']] (top) and the [[Star Wars Trilogy (DVD)|2004 DVD version]] (bottom)]]

The '''Aurebesh'''-like writing that appears in the [[original trilogy]] is totally random and it is believed that the filmmakers did not intend to write any meaningful text with it. The letters were first assigned Roman equivalents by [[Stephen Crane]] at [[West End Games]] in the ''[[Star Wars Miniatures Battles Companion]]'' ([[1994]]), for use with the ''[[Star Wars Miniatures Battles]]'' game and ''[[Star Wars: The Roleplaying Game]]''. The Aurebesh was later expanded to include punctuation marks in the ''[[Star Wars Miniatures Battles]]'' supplement, ''Imperial Entanglements'' ([[1996]]).

This ''original'' Aurebesh is occasionally used in electronic and board games such as ''[[Monopoly Star Wars (board game)|Monopoly Star Wars]]''. Since the letters in the movies are random, the assignment of the West End Games values to the inscriptions of the movies produces nonsensical results&mdash;most words seen in the movies appear to consist solely of consonants, and some letters appear on-screen that are absent from the West End Games Aurebesh.

In the [[2004]] DVD release of [[Star Wars: Episode IV A New Hope|''A New Hope'']], and the Blu-ray version, the words displaying information as [[Obi-Wan Kenobi/Legends|Obi-Wan Kenobi]] deactivates the [[Tractor beam/Legends|tractor beam]] on the [[DS-1 Orbital Battle Station/Legends|''Death Star'']], which were written using the [[High Galactic/Legends|Roman alphabet]] in previous releases, are now in the Aurebesh. Aurebesh can also be seen in the [[prequel trilogy]].

===Usage===
[[File:Aurebesh-GMSR.png|thumb|left|250px|Aurebesh letters and punctuation, from the Legends game accessory ''Star Wars Gamemaster Screen, Revised'']]
The word "Aurebesh" was developed in a manner similar to the word ''alphabet'', which is derived from the first two letters of the Phoenician/[[Tionese/Legends|Greek alphabet]] ([[alpha]] and [[beta]]).

[[In-universe]] sources show Arabic numbers; however, one of the fan-made fonts (discussed below) presents a numerical system based on dots and lines.

In many instances, the sounds "ch," "sh," and "th" are written using Aurebesh as they would be in English (cresh-herf, senth-herf, and trill-herf, respectively), despite separate letters existing in Aurebesh for those sounds (cherek, shen, and thesh, respectively). While it is possible that these instances represent legitimate in-universe variations of the sound-values for the letters in question, it is more likely that they represent errors on the part of the real-world transliterators (who are understandably more used to employing digraphs than employing single letters to write these sounds).
